subject: A-Level Business
scenario:
A company's sales rose from £18m to £21m.
Over the same period the total market grew from £150m to £200m.
question: Calculate the change in the company's market share. Show your working.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award marks as shown. Own Figure Rule (OFR) applies. Maximum 4 marks.
mark_scheme.answer: A fall of 1.5 percentage points (from 12% to 10.5%)
points: = a fall of 1.5 percentage points (1 mark)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept '-1.5%' or 'fall of 1.5%'. An answer of -12.5% (percentage change in share) is also creditworthy if clearly labelled as a percentage change.

formulae.math: Market share = business sales / total market sales x 100

examiner_principles: Award marks for correct working using the Own Figure Rule (OFR) - an arithmetic slip early on does not stop later method marks.
Correct formula with no valid calculation = 1 mark.
The final answer must be in the correct unit (units, %, days, £m, times, :1). Wrong unit, e.g. adding a £ sign to a number of units, loses the final mark.

subject: A-Level Business
question:
A business sells a product with a price elasticity of demand of -2.0 and an income elasticity of demand of +0.5. Next year consumer incomes are expected to fall and the business intends to increase its price.

Based solely on this information, analyse how the sales revenue for the product will change over the next year.

mark_scheme.instruction: Levels of response. Determine the level using the descriptors (best fit), then the mark within the level. Indicative content is not exhaustive - credit all valid lines of argument.
demands: interpreting PED of -2.0 (price elastic) and YED of +0.5 (normal good, income inelastic)
analysing the combined impact of falling incomes and a price rise on sales revenue
indicative_content: PED of -2.0 means a price rise causes a more than proportional fall in quantity demanded, e.g. a 5% price rise reduces quantity by about 10%, so revenue falls
YED of +0.5 means demand falls when incomes fall, but by a smaller percentage than the fall in incomes
both effects reduce quantity demanded, so sales revenue will fall
the effect of the price rise is likely to be larger than the income effect because demand is more responsive to price

subject: A-Level Business
topic: 3.3.4 Making marketing decisions: using the marketing mix
scenario:
Crestwell Coffee Ltd runs 46 coffee shops in towns across the Midlands and the North of England. It competes with national chains and independent cafés by focusing on high-quality, ethically sourced coffee. Its target market is professionals aged 25-45 who buy coffee on the way to work.

The business has opened four new shops in the last year, but the price of coffee beans has risen by 38% over two years and the National Living Wage rose by almost 10% in April 2024. Crestwell increased the price of a standard latte from £3.20 to £3.40, but directors fear that further price rises would drive customers to cheaper rivals.

Crestwell's marketing director wants to launch a monthly subscription: for £25 a month, subscribers could collect one hot drink per day. She believes it would 'lock in' loyal customers and attract new ones before a national rival launches a similar scheme. The finance director is less convinced.

only 28% rate price as very important - suggests demand is relatively price inelastic, so further price rises may be possible without large falls in sales
speed of service matters to 52%, especially 35+ (57%) - process and people decisions (more staff at peak, mobile ordering) to cut queues
18-34s value the app (58%) and ethical sourcing (55%) - promotion could emphasise ethical credentials via social media and app rewards
differences by age support different promotion for different segments
the survey only covers existing customers, so it may not show why non-customers choose rivals

Quantity is less important than focus: two well-developed, balanced arguments with a weighed judgement can reach the top level.
arguments_for: each subscriber pays £25 and costs about 18 x £0.62 = £11.16 in ingredients, giving a contribution of about £13.84 a month
the 30% of subscribers who are new customers (1 800) generate extra revenue of about £45 000 a month and may buy food too
ties customers in - 37% value loyalty rewards (58% of 18-34s) - and pre-empts the national rival
subscription revenue is paid in advance, improving cash flow
average capacity utilisation is only 64%, so extra visits outside the peak can be served at low marginal cost
arguments_against: 70% of subscribers (4 200) are existing regular customers: 18 drinks at £3.40 = £61.20 a month now, so each pays £36.20 less - roughly £152 000 of lost revenue a month
peak capacity utilisation is already 93%, so more morning visits could lengthen queues - speed matters to 52% of customers
only 28% of customers rate price as very important, so a discount scheme may give away margin unnecessarily
operating profit has already fallen to £1.5m and bean prices are rising - the scheme could make Crestwell loss-making
forecasts are estimates; the survey is of existing customers only
evaluation: the decision depends on the proportion of subscribers who are new customers and whether they buy extra items
Crestwell could limit the scheme (e.g. off-peak drinks only, or a higher price) to protect margins
a judgement should weigh the cannibalisation of existing revenue against the strategic threat from the rival

subject: A-Level Business
scenario:
Halden Furniture Ltd makes high-quality sofas to order in its factory in Lancashire. Customers choose the size, fabric and colour, and pay a 30% deposit when ordering. The remaining 70% is paid on delivery.

Orders have grown strongly, but the factory is running at 96% capacity utilisation and the average time between order and delivery has risen from 7 to 10 weeks. Rivals deliver in about 6 weeks. Halden holds large inventories of fabric 'just in case' customers choose them.

To reduce lead times, the directors are considering two options. Option 1: outsource the making of wooden sofa frames to a specialist supplier in Poland, freeing factory space for upholstery. Option 2: invest £1.2m in computer-controlled cutting machines, which would increase capacity by 25%.

subject: A-Level Business
scenario:
Background
Harbour & Hale plc (H&H) was founded in 1952 and has 180 clothing stores on UK high streets. It sells mid-priced women's and men's clothing to customers aged 35 to 60. For decades H&H was known for reliable quality and good customer service.

Over the last five years, H&H's market share has fallen steadily. Online-only retailers offer wider ranges and faster delivery, while discount chains offer lower prices. Footfall on many high streets has fallen. H&H launched a website in 2016, but it is slow and has few features. Online sales are 18% of H&H's revenue, compared with 38% for the clothing market as a whole.

New leadership
In 2024 H&H's long-serving chief executive retired. His successor, Marcus Bell, joined from an online retailer. He said: 'For too long this business has made small changes while our customers changed completely.'

Marcus has announced 'Project Renew': 60 stores will close, with 1 400 redundancies; £40m will be invested in an automated distribution centre to support online sales; and the brand will be relaunched to appeal to customers aged 25 to 45.

Institutional shareholders welcomed the plan and the share price rose 9%. The trade union representing shop workers has threatened strike action. Many store managers have worked for H&H for more than 20 years and do not trust the new management team.

The distribution centre
The distribution centre would allow next-day delivery across the UK. H&H's finance director has prepared the forecasts in Appendix C. She points out that the forecasts assume online sales will double within three years.
question: Using Appendix A, analyse the reasons for Harbour & Hale plc's falling market share.

mark_scheme.instruction: Levels of response. Determine the level using the descriptors (best fit), then the mark within the level. Indicative content is not exhaustive - credit all valid lines of argument.
demands: interpret Appendix A (share 1.9% to 1.4% while the market grew)
analyse reasons, in context
indicative_content: the market grew from £48bn to £55bn (+15%) but H&H's share fell from 1.9% to 1.4%, so its sales fell in absolute terms (about £0.91bn to £0.77bn)
online's share of the market rose from 27% to 38%; H&H's online sales are only 18% of its revenue with a slow website - it missed the main source of growth
falling high-street footfall hit H&H's 180 stores
competitors offer either lower prices (discounters) or wider ranges and faster delivery (online) - H&H is 'stuck in the middle'
H&H's ageing target market (35-60)
